source.title: Linguistic properties and model scale in brain encoding: from small to compressed language models
source.authors: S. Oota; Vijay Rowtula; Satya Sai Srinath Namburi; Khushbu Pahwa; Anant Khandelwal; Manish Gupta; Tanmoy Chakraborty; B. Raju

page_placements.theme: Human behavioral and brain alignment have measure-specific scaling

record.tranche_reason: The paper discusses language-model scaling laws as background, but its experiments measure brain encoding and decoding, not held-out pretraining cross-entropy, loss extrapolation, or compute-optimal allocation.
record.gate_note: The study scales model size and measures brain alignment, a related but different outcome from the loss-based claim. Those scale-comparison results are recorded with versions ["none"] and described under fits_no_version. The FlashHolmes scores do not test whether downstream performance can be predicted from pretraining loss or a fitted scaling law. The paper also reports compression effects on brain alignment, which do not test the listed claim versions.
record.test_reason: The study measures fMRI brain-encoding alignment, brain-to-text decoding and linguistic probing across model sizes and compression variants of pretrained base checkpoints. It reports no pretraining loss, fits no power law, does no extrapolation or compute-optimal allocation, and does not relate downstream scores to pretraining loss. Brain alignment versus parameter count is a related but different construct, so it goes under fits_no_version. Kaplan and Hoffmann are cited only as background.
record.authors_conclusion: Broadly correct. The authors conclude that brain alignment saturates around 3B parameters (1B to 1.5B models underperform) and is robust to most compression methods, with GPTQ the exception. They also report a dissociation between linguistic probing performance and brain alignment. They say the results do not overturn global scaling laws but show a local plateau in the 1B to 14B regime.
record.recipe_differences: The study measures fMRI brain-encoding alignment across model sizes and compression variants; it does not fit power laws to held-out pretraining loss, extrapolate loss, or optimize parameter/token allocation under a compute budget.
record.method_sensitivity: Brain-alignment results vary with model size and family, compression method, and dataset paradigm (listening versus reading). Analyses use the best-performing layer per model.

fits_no_version.finding: Across the Qwen2.5, LLaMA-3.2 and DeepSeek-R1 families (1B to 14B), 3B models' best-layer brain alignment is statistically indistinguishable from 7B to 14B, while 1B to 1.5B models are significantly worse. The 7B models are sometimes significantly below 3B and 14B, so the trend is non-monotonic.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: fMRI brain-encoding alignment of LMs saturates around 3B parameters rather than following a monotonic scaling trend.

fits_no_version.finding: On the reading fMRI dataset, Qwen2.5 3B alignment is comparable to 7B and 14B, while 1.5B shows a clear drop.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: The brain-alignment plateau around 3B generalises from the listening to the reading paradigm.

record.problems: The relevant outcomes are brain-alignment measures rather than language-model loss. The listening fMRI evaluation uses nine participants. The reading result is described qualitatively in the text and shown in a figure.
record.rows_left_out: Compression comparisons and FlashHolmes task-score results are not included as rows because they do not test any listed version of the loss-scaling claim. The paper's decoding metrics likewise measure brain-to-text reconstruction, not downstream-task predictability from pretraining loss.

untested.parts: No held-out pretraining loss is measured across parameters, tokens or compute.
No loss extrapolation from small runs.
No depth or width comparison of loss at a fixed parameter count.
No power-law loss fits in other modalities or training regimes.
FlashHolmes probing scores are reported by size but are not related to pretraining loss and no scaling fit is made. Brain alignment is not a downstream task of the claim's kind.
No fitted exponents or fitting choices are examined.

record.verdict_notes: I agree with the reader's T6/discusses classification. The compression, FlashHolmes and decoding results are correctly left out because none bears on any loss-scaling version. The LLaMA appendix tables label 7B and 14B models that are absent from Table 1, an internal inconsistency in the paper.

versions.untested_parts: Held-out pretraining loss as a function of parameters, tokens, or compute.
Prediction of large-run held-out loss from fitted small-run losses.
Effects of depth, width, or other architecture details on held-out loss at fixed parameter count.
Power-law loss forms in other modalities or training regimes.
Prediction of downstream performance from pretraining loss or scaling-law fits.
Dependence of loss-law exponents or compute-optimal allocation on setup and fitting choices.

relation.reason: It discusses language-model scaling laws and distinguishes its local brain-alignment plateau from global scaling laws; it does not test or use the cataloged laws.

tranche.reason: The study compares brain alignment and linguistic probing across checkpoints and compression methods, without testing a power-law form, loss extrapolation, compute-optimal allocation, or quantitative downstream scaling predictability.

source_check.notes: The paper contains inconsistent Qwen comparison statistics and LLaMA size labels; Table 1 lists an 8B LLaMA while Table 9 labels larger comparisons 7B/14B. Nonsignificant differences do not establish statistical equivalence.

statements.correction: Qwen2.5 Table 2: 3B–14B p = 1.00; 3B–7B p ≈ 0.06; 3B–1.5B p = 0.004. LLaMA Table 9: 3B–14B and 3B–7B labeled nonsignificant; 3B–1B p < 0.001. DeepSeek Table 10: 14B–3B p ≈ 0.61; 3B–7B ∆ = 0.08, t(8) = 4.18, p < 0.01; 3B–1B p < 0.001. Reading-dataset comparison: qualitative comparability of Qwen2.5 3B with 7B/14B and a drop at 1.5B.
statements.problem: The blanket statistical equivalence with 7B–14B overstates the results: DeepSeek 3B significantly outperforms 7B, although the authors broadly describe saturation near 3B.
